item.title: Atlantic Tropical Weather Outlook
item.description:
370
ABNT20 KNHC 291709
TWOAT

Tropical Weather Outlook
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL
200 PM EDT Tue Sep 29 2026

For the North Atlantic...Caribbean Sea and the Gulf of America:

Active Systems:
The National Hurricane Center is issuing advisories on Tropical
Depression Fay, located well to the west-southwest of the Azores,
and on Tropical Storm Hanna, located well to the east-northeast of
Bermuda.

Tropical cyclone formation is not expected over the next 7 days.

$$
Forecaster Kelly

----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...23.7N 48.2W
ABOUT 1590 MI...2560 KM WSW OF THE AZORES
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...30 MPH...45 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...WSW OR 240 DEGREES AT 12 MPH...19 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...1011 MB...29.86 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 500 PM AST (2100 UTC), the center of Post-Tropical Cyclone Fay 
was located near latitude 23.7 North, longitude 48.2 West. The 
post-tropical cyclone is moving toward the west-southwest near 12 
mph (19 km/h), and this motion is expected to continue for the next 
couple of days.
 
Maximum sustained winds are near 30 mph (45 km/h) with higher gusts. 
Little change in strength is forecast, and Fay is forecast to 
dissipate in a day or so.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 1011 mb (29.86 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
None.
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
This is the last public advisory issued by the National Hurricane 
Center on this system. Additional information on this system can be 
found in High Seas Forecasts issued by the National Weather Service, 
under AWIPS header NFDHSFAT1, WMO header FZNT01 KWBC, and online at 
ocean.weather.gov/shtml/NFDHSFAT1.php
 
$$
Forecaster Kelly

item.title: Post-Tropical Cyclone Fay Forecast Discussion Number 39
item.description:
Issued at 500 PM AST Tue Sep 29 2026 
000
WTNT41 KNHC 292034
TCDAT1
 
Post-Tropical Cyclone Fay Discussion Number  39
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL062026
500 PM AST Tue Sep 29 2026
 
Fay's time as a tropical cyclone has faded away. An earlier 
scatterometer pass showed that the system had weakened with maximum 
winds around 25 kt, and that the low-level center was becoming less 
defined. While occasional bursts of convection may continue, the 
convection has not been organized in several hours. Thus, the system 
is being designated as a post-tropical cyclone with an initial 
intensity of 25 kt.
 
The post-tropical cyclone will continue to move generally 
west-southwestward at around 10 kt, steered along the southern 
periphery of the mid-level ridge located over the central Atlantic. 
The system should continue to gradually weaken and is expected to 
dissipate into an open trough in about a day or so. The latest NHC 
track and intensity forecast is similar to the previous advisory and 
lies near the latest consensus aids.
 
This is the last public advisory issued by the National Hurricane 
Center on this system. Additional information on this system can be 
found in High Seas Forecasts issued by the National Weather Service, 
under AWIPS header NFDHSFAT1, WMO header FZNT01 KWBC, and online at 
ocean.weather.gov/shtml/NFDHSFAT1.php

SUMMARY OF 900 PM GMT...2100 UTC...INFORMATION
----------------------------------------------
LOCATION...34.0N 44.5W
ABOUT 1175 MI...1895 KM E OF BERMUDA
ABOUT 1015 MI...1630 KM W OF THE AZORES
MAXIMUM SUSTAINED WINDS...40 MPH...65 KM/H
PRESENT MOVEMENT...SE OR 125 DEGREES AT 12 MPH...19 KM/H
MINIMUM CENTRAL PRESSURE...1005 MB...29.68 INCHES
 
 
WATCHES AND WARNINGS
--------------------
There are no coastal watches or warnings in effect.
 
 
DISCUSSION AND OUTLOOK
----------------------
At 900 PM GMT (2100 UTC), the center of Tropical Storm Hanna was 
located near latitude 34.0 North, longitude 44.5 West. Hanna is 
moving toward the southeast near 12 mph (19 km/h) and and this 
motion is forecast to continue with a decrease in forward speed 
through Wednesday morning, followed by a turn to the east-northeast.
 
Maximum sustained winds are near 40 mph (65 km/h) with higher gusts. 
Gradual weakening is expected during the next couple of days, and 
Hanna is likely to become a post-tropical cyclone by Thursday.
 
Tropical-storm-force winds extend outward up to 70 miles (110 km)
from the center.
 
The estimated minimum central pressure is 1005 mb (29.68 inches).
 
 
HAZARDS AFFECTING LAND
----------------------
None.
 
 
NEXT ADVISORY
-------------
Next complete advisory at 300 AM GMT.
 
$$
Forecaster Beven

item.title: Tropical Storm Hanna Forecast Discussion Number 6
item.description:
Issued at 900 PM GMT Tue Sep 29 2026 
916 
WTNT43 KNHC 292032
TCDAT3
 
Tropical Storm Hanna Discussion Number   6
NWS National Hurricane Center Miami FL       AL082026
900 PM GMT Tue Sep 29 2026
 
Satellite imagery this afternoon shows that the low-level center of 
Hanna continues mostly exposed to the west of the main convective 
area. However, the convective area has become more elongated 
east-west and the system looks more frontal than it did six hours 
ago due to interaction with a frontal boundary near and to the east 
of the cyclone. Satellite intensity estimates have changed little 
since the last advisory, so the initial intensity remains 35 kt 
based on this and an earlier scatterometer overpass.
 
The initial motion is now 125/10 kt.  Hanna is located along the 
southern edge of the mid-latitude westerlies to the southwest of a 
large trough over the northeastern Atlantic.  This pattern is 
responsible for the current southeasterly motion.  During the next 
12-24 h, the flow near the cyclone become more west-to-east, and as 
Hanna weakens vertically a low-level ridge centered south of the 
Azores will become the main steering influence. This should result 
in the cyclone or its remnants turning east-northeastward.  The new 
forecast track is nudged a little to the south of the previous track 
due mainly to the initial position and motion.
  
Hanna should gradually weaken due to shear, dry air entrainment, and 
possible merger with the frontal boundary.  The latest GFS/ECMWF 
simulated satellite imagery now forecasts the system to stop 
producing convection at around 36 h, at which time it would 
degenerate to a remnant low.  After that, the remnant low is 
expected to weaken to a trough by 96 h.
